changes.from: I can walk a long way
changes.to: I can go on a hike
changes.why: The cue shows a child hiking with a backpack and poles; 'walk a long way' is vague (how far?) and does not name what the picture shows. 'Go on a hike' is a clean yes/no a kindergartner can answer.

changes.from: I can put on my coat
changes.why: Same sheet already has 'I can put on my boots' and 'I can get dressed' — three dressing sentences in one frame. The coat picture has big buttons, and buttoning is a real K fine-motor milestone (a genuine yes/no), unlike putting a coat on, which nearly every 5-year-old can do.
The cue picture is a broom; the sentence must say what the picture shows or a pre-reader guesses from the picture and misreads. 'Help tidy up' is also a yes for every child.

changes.to: I can color in the lines
changes.why: Same sheet (school) has 'I can paint a picture' — two sentences ending 'a picture' side by side. The cue is a crayon; coloring in the lines is the classic US K crayon skill and a real yes/no (US spelling 'color').
The play sheet had three 'I can play …' sentences (drum, guitar, board game). 'Drum a beat' keeps the verb distinct and is a skill K music class actually practices.
US 5-year-olds say 'take a picture'; 'photo' is adult/British-leaning register.
'Swing high' is not a yes/no (every child swings high when pushed). Swinging without a push (pumping your legs) is the real K milestone.

changes.from: I can skip with a rope
changes.why: 'Skip with a rope' is British English; in the US, 'skip' means the hop-step gait, so a US child reads this as something else. The move sheet now reuses this shipped string on a new worksheet — fix it in the shipped en block too (18 → 15 chars).

optionWordFlags.problem: The picture is ONE large round red cherry with a short stem — at tile size it reads as a red apple, and 'apple' is in the same row. A child who circles it and copies 'cherry' may think they chose an apple. Drop it, or use a picture showing the usual pair of cherries on joined stems.

US children do not call this porridge; they say 'oatmeal' (the word is known mainly from Goldilocks). Swap to breakfast/oatmeal (same kind of bowl, has a spoon) if its vocab label is 'oatmeal'; otherwise keep porridge — it is correct, just less familiar.
Not a real problem for a favorite-shape row (kids happily pick a moon), but note it is a crescent, not a geometric shape name; it is fine as long as the sheet never teaches shape names from this row.
Correct picture and word, but it is the hardest word in any row to copy (9 letters, silent t). Acceptable; mention only if the panel wants every copy word short.
Not insects — which is exactly why the heading says 'bug', not 'insect'. Keep 'bug' in English; other locales must choose a heading word that also covers them (flag for the non-EN panels).

designNotes: Heading length: 'My favorite farm animal' is 23 characters, one over the 22 target. It is the only natural wording (no shorter US phrase keeps the pattern); test that it fits in two lines at the box width, and keep it if it does.

Headings kept deliberately: 'bug' (not 'insect', because the row has a snail, spider and worm); 'treat' (covers cake, lollipop, popsicle, waffle); 'clothes' (plural is how US kids talk: 'my favorite clothes'); 'hobby' is a slightly big word for a 5-year-old but the teacher reads the heading aloud and the pictures carry it.
Duplicate pictures across categories are fine because they never share a worksheet: parrot (pet set 2, bird set 4), rabbit (pet set 2, farm set 6), pancake + muffin (treat set 3, breakfast set 5).

activities/baking (cue for 'I can help bake a cake') shows an ADULT chef — the shipped K-323 header notes this picture was rejected for exactly that reason. The sentence says 'help', so it still works, but consider a child-baking picture or a kitchen-object cue (whisk, mixing bowl) if one exists.

activities/hiking, toys/slide, toys/swing, weather/puddle, camping/fishing_rod, around the house/watering_can, faucet, comb, bed and broom all match their sentences once the changes above are applied. around the house/comb is drawn as a comb-on-a-handle; still reads as comb.
Move sheet has 'I can kick a ball' (shipped soccer) and 'I can bounce a ball' side by side — different verbs, acceptable; do not also add 'throw a ball' later.
Self sheet after changes: brush teeth / comb hair / wash hands / get dressed / button coat / put on boots / make bed / sweep floor — no two sentences share a verb.
Play sheet after changes: sing a song / drum a beat / play the guitar / build a tower / play a board game / help bake a cake / take a picture / fly a kite — 'play' now appears twice, down from three.
All 27 sentences: first person, no digits, no '{', max 24 characters ('I can color in the lines'); each is a real yes/no for a 5-6-year-old.
